#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
#include <stack>
using namespace std;

const int MAXN = 1000; // since 2*n <= 1000

vector<int> G[MAXN], Gr[MAXN];
bool visited[MAXN];
int comp[MAXN];
stack<int> order;

void dfs1(int u) {
    visited[u] = true;
    for (int v : G[u]) {
        if (!visited[v]) {
            dfs1(v);
        }
    }
    order.push(u);
}

void dfs2(int u, int cl) {
    comp[u] = cl;
    for (int v : Gr[u]) {
        if (comp[v] == -1) {
            dfs2(v, cl);
        }
    }
}

int main() {
    int t;
    cin >> t;
    while (t--) {
        int n;
        cin >> n;
        // clear graphs
        for (int i=0; i<2*n; i++) {
            G[i].clear();
            Gr[i].clear();
            visited[i] = false;
            comp[i] = -1;
        }
        while (!order.empty()) order.pop();

        // read grid
        vector<vector<int>> grid(3, vector<int>(n));
        for (int i=0; i<3; i++) {
            for (int j=0; j<n; j++) {
                cin >> grid[i][j];
            }
        }

        // for each column j
        for (int j=0; j<n; j++) {
            vector<int> lits;
            for (int i=0; i<3; i++) {
                int v = grid[i][j];
                int idx;
                if (v > 0) {
                    idx = 2 * (v-1);
                } else {
                    idx = 2 * (-v-1) + 1;
                }
                lits.push_back(idx);
            }
            // now have three literals
            vector<pair<int,int>> pairs = { {0,1}, {0,2}, {1,2} };
            for (auto p : pairs) {
                int a = lits[p.first];
                int b = lits[p.second];
                if (a == b) {
                    // unit clause: add edge from neg(a) to a
                    int na = (a % 2 == 0) ? a+1 : a-1;
                    G[na].push_back(a);
                    Gr[a].push_back(na);
                } else if (a == neg(b)) {
                    // tautology, skip
                    continue;
                } else {
                    int na = (a % 2 == 0) ? a+1 : a-1;
                    int nb = (b % 2 == 0) ? b+1 : b-1;
                    G[na].push_back(b);
                    Gr[b].push_back(na);
                    G[nb].push_back(a);
                    Gr[a].push_back(nb);
                }
            }
        }

        // Now compute SCC using Kosaraju
        for (int i=0; i<2*n; i++) {
            if (!visited[i]) {
                dfs1(i);
            }
        }

        int cl = 0;
        while (!order.empty()) {
            int u = order.top();
            order.pop();
            if (comp[u] == -1) {
                dfs2(u, cl);
                cl++;
            }
        }

        // Check for conflict
        bool possible = true;
        for (int i=0; i<n; i++) {
            if (comp[2*i] == comp[2*i+1]) {
                possible = false;
                break;
            }
        }
        cout << (possible ? "YES" : "NO") << endl;
    }
}

question:
Permutation Counting

Time limit: 2000 ms
Memory limit: 256 MB
Rating: 1400

Description

You have some cards. An integer between $1$ and $n$ is written on each card: specifically, for each $i$ from $1$ to $n$, you have $a_i$ cards which have the number $i$ written on them. There is also a shop which contains unlimited cards of each type. You have $k$ coins, so you can buy $k$ new cards in total, and the cards you buy can contain any integer between $1$ and $n$. After buying the new cards, you rearrange all your cards in a line. The score of a rearrangement is the number of (contiguous) subarrays of length $n$ which are a permutation of $[1, 2, \ldots, n]$. What's the maximum score you can get?

Input

Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases $t\ (1\le t\le 100)$. The description of the test cases follows. The first line of each test case contains two integers $n$, $k$ ($1\le n \le 2 \cdot 10^5$, $0\le k \le 10^{12}$) — the number of distinct types of cards and the number of coins. The second line of each test case contains $n$ integers $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$ ($1 \le a_i \le 10^{12}$) — the number of cards of type $i$ you have at the beginning. It is guaranteed that the sum of $n$ over all test cases does not exceed $5 \cdot 10^5$.

Output

For each test case, output a single line containing an integer: the maximum score you can get.

Examples

Example 1

Note

In the second test case, we can buy $0$ cards of type $1$ and $4$ cards of type $2$, and then we rearrange the cards as following: $[1, 2, 1, 2, 1, 2, 1, 2, 1, 2, 1, 2, 1, 2, 1, 2]$. There are $8$ subarrays equal to $[1, 2]$ and $7$ subarrays equal to $[2, 1]$, which make a total of $15$ subarrays which are a permutation of $[1, 2]$. It can also be proved that this is the maximum score we can get. In the third test case, one of the possible optimal rearrangements is $[3, 3, 1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3, 1, 3]$.

The second line of each test case contains the $n$ integers $p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_n$ ($1 \leq p_i \leq n$). It is guaranteed that $p$ is a permutation of length $n$. It is guaranteed that the sum of $n$ across all test cases doesn't exceed $10^5$.

Output

It can be proven that this score is optimal under the constraints. In the last example, the resulting array $a = [6, 6, 12, 7, 14, 7, 14, 6]$ has $3$ local maximums — on the third, fifth and seventh positions.
